subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage: Monday. Maria, five, pushed Simran off the swing. The teacher frowned, and Maria went pale. "Am I bad now? Will I get a punishment?" Wednesday. Simran grabbed Maria's crayon. Maria's hand went up, then she looked at the teacher's desk and dropped it. "No hitting," she whispered. "Teacher gets angry." Friday. At home, Nani asked Maria why hitting is wrong. "Because you get punished," Maria said firmly. "That's the rule." "And if nobody saw?" Maria thought very hard, swinging her legs. "Then it's still the rule, Nani. Rules are just there."

qa.q: What did Maria do on Monday?
qa.a: She pushed Simran off the swing.

qa.q: What was Maria worried about when the teacher frowned?
qa.a: She worried she was bad now and that she would get a punishment.

qa.q: What choice did Maria make on Wednesday, and what was it based on?
qa.a: She dropped her raised hand instead of hitting Simran, because she expected the teacher to get angry.

qa.q: What might change if Nani asked Maria how Simran felt after the push?
qa.a: Maria might begin to notice that hitting hurts Simran, not only that it makes adults angry.

grounding: A five-year-old explains that hitting is wrong because you get punished and treats the rule as simply there, judging right by adult anger.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage: Rain kept the whole kindergarten indoors, and the teacher had stepped out to fetch towels. Omkar snatched Hemant's toy truck. Hemant's fist came up. Then he looked at the door. It was empty. He still stopped. "Hitting is bad," he told Omkar in a loud whisper. "Why?" said Omkar. "'Cause Miss gets angry and you sit in the corner chair." "But Miss isn't here." Hemant's forehead crinkled. He looked at the door again, then at the corner chair, as if the chair itself might tell on him. "The corner knows," he said, and put both hands behind his back.

qa.q: Why had the teacher stepped out?
qa.a: To fetch towels.

qa.q: What does Hemant's look at the corner chair suggest he felt?
qa.a: He seemed afraid of punishment even with Miss away, as if the corner chair itself could catch him.

qa.q: What could Miss do when she comes back to build on Hemant's choice?
qa.a: She could praise him for keeping his hands back and ask how Omkar might feel if hit, so his reason grows beyond the corner chair.

qa.q: Why might Omkar question Hemant's reason?
qa.a: Omkar noticed Miss was not in the room, so the threat of the corner seemed empty to Omkar.

grounding: A kindergartner holds back from hitting because the teacher gets angry and the corner punishes, treating the rule as a fixed fact even when no adult is present.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage: Kiran, five, came up three floors in the lift, crying. "Salma hit me! Ammi, she's very bad now. Watchman uncle will tell her mummy and she'll get a big scolding." Ammi wiped his face with her dupatta. "Is hitting wrong only because of the scolding?" Kiran looked at her as if she had asked why the sky was up. "Hitting is wrong because you get punished, Ammi. Everybody knows." "And if nobody scolded her?" He thought about it, then shook his head. "Somebody always scolds."

qa.q: Who did Kiran say would tell Salma's mummy?
qa.a: Watchman uncle.

qa.q: How did Kiran feel about Ammi's question, judging by his look?
qa.a: He was puzzled by it, as if the rule about hitting were as plain a fact as the sky being up.

qa.q: What could Ammi try next to help Kiran look beyond the scolding?
qa.a: She could ask how the hit felt to him, so he links hitting with hurt rather than only with punishment.

qa.q: What would change if Ammi had simply promised to get Salma scolded?
qa.a: Kiran would learn even more firmly that right and wrong depend on an adult's anger, instead of starting to think about why hitting hurts.

grounding: A five-year-old says hitting is wrong because you get punished and cannot imagine a world where no one scolds, treating the rule as a fact.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage:
"Dadi, Chintu hit me with the spoon!"
Urmila Dadi looked up from the peas. "And what did you do, Sumit?"
"Nothing. I didn't hit back." He puffed out his chest. "Hitting is bad."
"Why is it bad?"
"Because Mummy gets angry. And then no cartoons."
"What if Mummy is at the office?"
Sumit frowned hard. "Then... still bad. Still no cartoons. Later."
"And Chintu? He's only two."
"He'll get a big scolding when he's big," Sumit said, very sure. "That's the rule."
Dadi pulled him onto her lap. "Show me your arm. Does it hurt where the spoon went?"

qa.q: What did Chintu hit Sumit with?
qa.a: Chintu hit him with the spoon.

qa.q: Why does Sumit think hitting is bad?
qa.a: He thinks it is bad because Mummy gets angry and the cartoons stop, so right and wrong mean whether a grown-up will be cross.

qa.q: What could Dadi try next to help Sumit look beyond the scolding?
qa.a: Asking about his sore arm is a good start; she could gently link it to how the spoon hurt, so hitting is wrong because it hurts someone.

qa.q: How might Chintu, who is only two, understand the rule Sumit is so sure about?
qa.a: At two, Chintu probably has no idea there is a rule at all, so Sumit's certainty about a future scolding means nothing to him yet.

grounding: A five-year-old judges hitting wrong because Mummy gets angry and cartoons stop, treating the rule as a fixed fact.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage:
Nursery note, Tuesday. Written by Neelam, class teacher.
At water time Swati, four, saw Dev push Mahi off the bench. She ran to me first. "Dev did pushing! Now you will be angry?" I asked why pushing is wrong. She thought hard. "Because teacher gets angry. And no star." When I asked what if I hadn't seen, she looked puzzled, as if a rule simply is, like rain.
Later she checked my face before taking her turn on the slide.
Next step: at circle time I'll ask the children how Mahi felt, and read the story about the hurt rabbit. I mentioned it to her mother at pickup; this is very usual at four.

qa.q: What did Swati say would happen because of the pushing?
qa.a: She said the teacher gets angry and there would be no star.

qa.q: What does Swati's puzzled look suggest about how she sees rules?
qa.a: It suggests she feels a rule simply is, like rain, and hasn't thought that pushing could be wrong even if no teacher saw it.

qa.q: How could Neelam support Swati at circle time?
qa.a: By asking how Mahi felt and reading the hurt-rabbit story, Neelam can help Swati link pushing to someone getting hurt, not only to an angry teacher.

qa.q: How might Mahi feel if everyone only talked about the teacher being angry?
qa.a: Mahi might feel the fall itself was forgotten, since all the attention went to the rule and not to the one who got pushed. 🥺

grounding: A teacher's note records a four-year-old judging pushing wrong only because the teacher will be angry, treating the rule as a plain fact.
